transcript.content: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?

I finally agreed to come in because I just don’t care about the things that usually keep me balanced. Sailing races, my Saturday shift with the historical society, even working in my woodshop—they all feel like chores now. I keep putting them off.
About how long have you been feeling this loss of interest in your usual activities?
Since the scaffold accident during the business readjustment—so, a little over a year now.
Do you find yourself having unwanted, distressing memories or nightmares about the scaffold accident?

Yes. It can just hit me out of nowhere—I’ll see the scaffold dropping, clear as a photograph. Metal clanking or a backup alarm can set it off. Then for a few minutes I have trouble staying focused on the meeting or conversation I’m in.
Do you find yourself going out of your way to avoid places, people, or thoughts that remind you of the accident?

Yeah. I’ve gotten pretty good at routing my day so I don’t have to go near that coastal site or the harbor walkways by the cranes. And if people start talking through what went wrong, I usually find a way to step out of the conversation.
Since the accident, do you find yourself constantly on guard or unusually watchful for potential danger?
I’m not really sure what you mean by constantly on guard. I haven’t especially noticed that, no.
Have you noticed that you startle much more easily or feel jumpy when there are unexpected noises or sudden movements?
Yeah. If someone drops a metal ladder or a truck gate slams, I jump really hard before I can stop it. My heart keeps racing longer than it seems like it should afterward.
